objectives: Explain the differences between CISC and RISC processors and where each is used
Describe GPUs and their uses, including general-purpose (non-graphics) applications
Apply knowledge of multicore and parallel processing to justify a processor choice for a given workload

retrieval.q: From 1.1.1, what is the key feature of the Von Neumann architecture?
retrieval.a: A single shared memory and bus for both data and instructions.

retrieval.q: From 1.1.1, which architecture can fetch an instruction at the same time as reading/writing data, and why?
retrieval.a: Harvard, because it has separate memories and buses for instructions and data.

retrieval.q: From 1.1.1, why does adding more cores not always improve performance?
retrieval.a: Only if the task can be parallelised and the software supports it; sequential or dependent tasks gain little.

retrieval.q: From 1.1.1, what does the width of the address bus determine?
retrieval.a: The maximum number of addressable memory locations, calculated as 2^n.

retrieval.q: From 1.1.1, what is pipelining and what does it improve?
retrieval.a: Overlapping the fetch, decode and execute stages of consecutive instructions, increasing instruction throughput.

keywords.def: Complex Instruction Set Computer; many complex variable-length instructions with complexity in hardware; used in x86 desktops.
Reduced Instruction Set Computer; few simple fixed-length instructions aiming for one cycle each; used in ARM mobile/embedded.
Many-core processor that applies the same operation to large blocks of data in parallel (data parallelism).
General-purpose computing on a GPU for non-graphics tasks such as machine learning, simulation and hashing.
A chip containing two or more independent cores, each able to run its own fetch-decode-execute cycle.
Carrying out multiple computations simultaneously by splitting a task across cores.
Applying the same operation to many independent data items at the same time.
When one step needs the result of a previous step, forcing the work to run sequentially.

content.heading: CISC vs RISC
points: CISC has many complex, variable-length, multi-cycle instructions with complexity in hardware; RISC has few simple, fixed-length instructions aiming for one cycle each
RISC is easier to pipeline (uniform, single-cycle instructions) and uses less power, making it ideal for battery devices
Typical use: CISC in x86 desktops/laptops; RISC in ARM mobile phones and embedded systems

content.heading: Where the complexity lies
points: CISC keeps complexity in hardware, so each task needs fewer instructions and less compiler effort
RISC pushes complexity to the software/compiler, so programs need more instructions and more RAM
Modern x86 chips internally translate CISC instructions into RISC-like micro-ops

content.heading: GPUs and GPGPU
points: A GPU has thousands of small cores applying the same operation to large data sets in parallel (data parallelism)
Graphics use: transforming and shading many pixels/vertices of a 3D scene simultaneously
GPGPU (non-graphics) uses: machine-learning/neural-network training, scientific simulation, image/video processing, crypto hashing

content.heading: Multicore and parallel systems
points: Multicore CPUs contain several independent cores that can process instructions at the same time
Parallel processing splits a task across cores, but the software must be written to use them
Tasks parallelise poorly with data dependency, coordination overhead or an inherently sequential algorithm (limited by the serial fraction)

worked_example.title: Choosing CPU vs GPU for a data-parallel workload
steps: Identify the workload: the same calculation applied to millions of independent data points with little branching
Recognise this as highly data-parallel, which suits many small cores working simultaneously
Match to a GPU: thousands of cores maximise throughput across the data points in parallel
Note the caveat: the software must be written to use the GPU, and very branchy/dependent code would suit a CPU
Conclude with justification: the GPU is the better choice here because it processes far more data points at once

task: Produce a comparison table for CISC vs RISC (instruction set, instruction length, cycles per instruction, where the complexity lies, power, typical use), then write one or two sentences on when a GPU beats a multicore CPU and why.
challenge: A program sorts a list and then searches it, and the search cannot begin until the sort finishes. Explain, using the terms data dependency and serial fraction, why running this on a multicore CPU gives only limited speed-up.

exit_ticket.q: Give one reason RISC is preferred in mobile phones.
exit_ticket.a: It uses lower power (simple fixed-length instructions), extending battery life; it is also easier to pipeline.

exit_ticket.q: Why is a GPU faster than a CPU for rendering 3D graphics?
exit_ticket.a: It has thousands of small cores that process many pixels/vertices in parallel rather than sequentially.

exit_ticket.q: Why do some tasks gain little from extra cores?
exit_ticket.a: Data dependency or an inherently sequential algorithm forces steps to run one after another, and coordination adds overhead (the serial fraction limits speed-up).
